meta.title: Markaestro for AI Agents | Connect an MCP Client or Use an API Key
meta.description: Connect Claude Code, Claude, Cursor, ChatGPT, Grok, OpenClaw, Hermes, or any MCP client to Markaestro with a browser sign-in, or hand an agent a brand-scoped API key. Discover connected social accounts, upload media, draft, schedule, and publish across Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn, Threads, Pinterest, and X.
meta.ogDescription: One sign-in or one API key turns Markaestro into a publishing tool your agent can call: discover accounts, upload media, draft, schedule, publish, and report back.

hero.title: Connect your agent in one step. It runs your social channels.
hero.intro1: Markaestro is built to be operated by software. An MCP client such as Claude Code, Cursor, ChatGPT, or Grok signs in through the browser and is handed a key bound to one brand; any other agent gets the same key from Settings. Either way the agent can discover which accounts it can post to, upload media, draft and schedule posts, publish them, and report back on what actually shipped, across Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn, Threads, Pinterest, and X.
hero.intro2: No SDK to install and no platform credentials to babysit. Your team connects the accounts once in the dashboard; the agent talks to one bearer-token API from then on.

why.eyebrow: Designed for Autonomy, Bounded on Purpose
why.title: Why an API Key Is the Whole Integration
why.intro: The hard part of letting an agent touch social media is not the HTTP. It is making sure a confused model cannot post to the wrong brand, double-post on a retry, or ship something nobody read. Those guarantees are in the API surface itself, not in your prompt.

cards.title: One Key, One Brand
cards.body: Every API key is bound to a single brand when you create it. An agent holding that key can only ever see and post to that brand, cross-brand requests are rejected at authentication, not by convention.

cards.title: Discovery, Not Hardcoded IDs
cards.body: The agent asks which accounts it can post to and gets back opaque ids to pass straight back. No Page ids, no Business Manager spelunking, no config file that rots when a connection is re-linked.

cards.title: Idempotent Writes
cards.body: Send an Idempotency-Key on any create or publish. A retried call inside 24 hours replays the original response instead of creating a second post, the failure mode agents hit most.

cards.title: A Human Stays in the Loop
cards.body: Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok posts are manual-first: your agent prepares them, a person posts them natively. Nothing goes out unattended unless you explicitly opt that post in.

loop.title: Five Calls, Start to Finish
loop.intro: Every Markaestro automation is a variation on this loop. Steps one through three are the Connect API, the flat surface most agents should target. Steps four and five reach into the full /api/public/v1 API for explicit publishing and run tracking.

steps.title: Discover
steps.body: Returns every connected, publishable account for the key's brand, each with a platform, username, and an opaque id. Call it at the start of a run, connections change.

steps.title: Upload Media
steps.body: Mint a short-lived, single-use signed URL, then PUT the raw bytes to it. You get back a media id. Images up to 10 MB; the full API also takes video up to 250 MB.

steps.title: Draft or Schedule
steps.body: Pass the caption, the media ids, and the account ids verbatim. Leave it a draft for review, or send is_draft false with scheduled_at to put it on the calendar.

steps.title: Publish
steps.body: Queues an async run. LinkedIn, Threads, Pinterest, and X go out over the official API. Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok land in the workspace's To post queue for a human to post natively.

steps.title: Report Back
steps.body: Poll the run id, or register a webhook endpoint and let Markaestro push post.published, post.action_required, and post.failed to you. Never assume a publish finished synchronously.

quickstart.title: A Working Integration in Four Commands
quickstart.intro: First, mint the key: open <settingsLink>Settings → API</settingsLink>, pick the brand it is allowed to touch, tick the scopes it needs, and optionally give it an expiry. The key is shown once, put it straight into your agent's secret store. Creating keys requires an admin or owner with a verified email.

step1.title: 1. Discover the accounts
step1.description: The first call in every run. Connections change; ids should never be baked into a prompt.

step2.title: 2. Upload the media
step2.description: Two steps: mint a signed, single-use URL, then PUT the bytes. The URL expires after 15 minutes and needs no auth header of its own.

step3.title: 3. Schedule it, then watch it
step3.description: Creating is draft-first by default. Send is_draft: false with a scheduled_at timestamp to put the post on the calendar instead.

toolDefs.title: Tool Definitions and an Agent Brief
toolDefs.intro: Two things to copy. The first is a set of tool schemas covering the whole publishing loop, written in JSON Schema, so they work as Claude tool definitions, OpenAI functions, or the input shape for an MCP server you host. The second is the operating brief that keeps a model from doing something surprising with them.
toolDefs.schemasDescription: Core posting tools: list accounts, upload media, create, publish, list, and delete. The hosted MCP server also includes Intelligent Evergreen, run history, bulk operations, and webhooks.
toolDefs.briefDescription: Paste into your system prompt. It encodes the behaviors that separate a reliable publishing agent from one that double-posts and declares victory early.
toolDefs.briefFooter: Your agent can also fetch this itself: curl https://markaestro.com/llms.txt returns a plain-text brief of the whole API, endpoints, rules, and error handling, small enough to sit in context.

recipes.title: The Four Workflows Agents Actually Run

publish.title: Publish and Confirm
publish.description: Create a draft, publish it explicitly, then poll the run. The only honest way to tell the operator a post went out.

audit.title: Audit and Cancel the Queue
audit.description: List what is scheduled, show it to a human, delete what they reject. Both calls use scopes an existing key already carries.

batch.title: Fill a Week in One Call
batch.description: Batch create takes up to 25 posts and returns per-item results, so a single malformed item does not sink the run.

webhook.title: Get Called Instead of Polling
webhook.description: Long-running agents should register a webhook and sleep. Deliveries are HMAC-signed with a secret shown once at creation.

guardrails.title: What the Agent Can and Cannot Do
guardrails.intro: Autonomy is only useful if the blast radius is small. Markaestro's defaults assume the caller is software that might be wrong.
guardrails.calloutTitle: Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok Are Manual-First
guardrails.calloutBody: Posts your agent creates for those channels default to manual_reminder: Markaestro never calls the platform's API for them. Publishing moves the post into the workspace's To post queue, where a person downloads the media, posts natively, and confirms, so the post looks exactly like it was made by hand, and a human sees every one before it exists publicly. An agent can opt a single post into official-API publishing with deliveryMode: "direct_publish", and on TikTok that means the creator-inbox handoff, never an unattended public post. LinkedIn, Threads, Pinterest, and X publish programmatically once your agent explicitly asks.

items.title: Scope the Key Down
items.body: Pick only the scopes the agent needs: products.read, media.write, posts.read, posts.write, posts.publish, evergreen.read, evergreen.write, analytics.read, job_runs.read, webhooks.manage. A research agent that only reads the calendar and the numbers gets posts.read and analytics.read and nothing else.

items.title: Give It an Expiry
items.body: Keys can be created with an expiry. An expired key behaves exactly like a revoked one, so a key that leaks out of an agent's environment stops working on its own.

items.title: Rotate and Revoke
items.body: Rotate a key in place or revoke it outright from Settings → API. Every key shows its last-used time and request volume, so an agent that goes quiet, or goes rogue, is visible.

items.title: Rate Limits Are Enforced
items.body: 60 requests per minute per endpoint and 240 per minute per key. Every response carries X-RateLimit-Limit, -Remaining, and -Reset; a 429 carries Retry-After. Honor it rather than hammering.

items.title: Markaestro Never Writes for You
items.body: There is no generation step. The caption comes from your agent, the media comes from your library or your agent's pipeline. Markaestro is the hands, not the voice.

items.title: Deletes Are Markaestro-Side
items.body: Deleting a scheduled post cancels it before it ships. Deleting a published post only stops Markaestro tracking it, the live post stays up until someone removes it on the platform.

errors.title: Teach it which errors are worth retrying
errors.intro: Every error response is JSON with a stable error code and a requestId. Have your agent quote the requestId when it reports a failure, it is what support needs to trace the call.

rows.action: Key is missing, revoked, or expired. Stop and ask a human for a new one. Retrying will not help.
The key lacks the scope for this call. Report which call failed; scopes are changed in Settings → API.
A key issued before brand binding. Ask for a replacement key.
The payload broke a channel rule (missing media, bad delivery mode, wrong scheduled_at). Fix the request; do not retry unchanged.
The same Idempotency-Key was sent with a different body. Mint a new key per distinct request.
Tried to delete a post while a publish run is in flight. Wait for the run to settle, then delete.
A publish run for this post is already queued. Do not publish again. Poll the existing run instead.
No active plan is attached to this workspace. Ask a workspace owner to review billing in Settings.
The workspace hit its monthly upload quota. Stop uploading and surface it. Existing media still publishes.
The id is outside this key's brand. Answered as 404 rather than 403 so keys cannot probe for ids they do not own.
Sleep for Retry-After seconds, then retry the same request with the same Idempotency-Key.

stacks.title: If It Can Make an HTTPS Request, It Can Publish
stacks.intro: There is no Markaestro client library to adopt and no framework to standardize on. Bearer token, JSON in, JSON out.

items.name: Claude & the Claude Agent SDK
items.body: Drop the tool definitions above into your tool list. The JSON Schema shapes are already in Claude tool-use format.

items.name: OpenAI Function Calling
items.body: The same schemas map one-to-one onto function definitions. Rename input_schema to parameters.

items.name: MCP Clients
items.body: Claude Code, Claude, Cursor, ChatGPT, Grok, Grok Bot, OpenClaw, Hermes: add the hosted server URL and sign in through the browser. For stdio-only clients, npx -y @markaestro/mcp runs the same thirty-one tools locally.

items.name: n8n, Make, Zapier
items.body: Every endpoint is a plain HTTP request with a bearer token. No SDK, no signing ceremony, no OAuth dance for the agent.

items.name: LangChain & LlamaIndex
items.body: Standard REST tools. The two-step media upload is the only multi-call flow, and it is two lines.

items.name: A cron job and curl
items.body: Not every agent needs a framework. The quickstart above is a complete, working integration in four commands.

cta.title: Give Your Agent Something Real to Do
cta.subtitle: Connect your channels, then connect your agent: sign in from Claude Code, Cursor, ChatGPT, Grok, OpenClaw, or Hermes, or mint a brand-scoped key. Either one is the entire integration.

mcp.title: Sign in from the client. Nothing to paste.
mcp.intro1: Claude Code, Claude, Cursor, ChatGPT, Grok, Grok Bot, OpenClaw, Hermes, and every other client that speaks the Model Context Protocol can connect to Markaestro's hosted MCP server with no credentials configured. The first tool call opens your browser: sign in, choose the workspace and the brand the agent may act on, review the permissions, and click Allow. The client receives a key bound to that brand and refreshes it on its own.
mcp.intro2: This is standard OAuth 2.1 with PKCE and dynamic client registration, the same mechanism behind other hosted MCP servers, so it works without a Markaestro-specific plugin. The server lives at https://markaestro.com/api/public/v1/mcp and exposes thirty-one tools over the public API: brand and destination discovery, media upload, draft and scheduled posts, brand analytics and per-post metric history, Intelligent Evergreen analytics, publishing with job-run polling, bulk operations, webhooks, and the per-channel rules.
mcp.flowTitle: What Happens When the Client Connects
mcp.flowIntro: Five steps, all of them handled by the client and the browser. You see only the consent page.

steps.title: Challenge
steps.body: The client calls the MCP endpoint without a credential. Markaestro answers 401 with a WWW-Authenticate header that names the protected-resource metadata document. That header is what tells the client a sign-in is available.

steps.title: Discovery
steps.body: The client reads two public documents: which authorization server protects the endpoint, and where that server's registration, authorization, and token endpoints are. Both are served on markaestro.com and cacheable.

steps.title: Registration
steps.body: The client registers itself with a name and its callback address. Loopback addresses, https callbacks, and native app schemes are accepted; plain http to a real host is refused. No pre-shared client id is needed.

steps.title: Consent
steps.body: Your browser opens the consent page. A workspace owner or admin with a verified email picks the workspace and brand, adjusts the permissions, and clicks Allow. Markaestro sends the browser back to the client with a single-use code.

steps.title: Token
steps.body: The client exchanges the code plus its PKCE verifier for an access token and a refresh token. The access token is an ordinary workspace API key bound to the chosen brand. It expires after 30 days; a refresh rotates its secret and extends it for another 30.

facts.title: The Token Is a Real API Key
facts.body: Scopes, brand binding, rate limits, subscription checks, idempotency, and revocation are the same code path as a key created by hand. There is no second permission model to reason about.

facts.title: Listed and Revocable in Settings
facts.body: A connected agent shows in Settings, API with a Connected agent badge, its last-used time, and its request volume. Revoke it there and the client's next call fails; the client can also revoke its own token when you disconnect it.

facts.title: One Connection, One Brand
facts.body: Every connection is bound to exactly one brand, chosen at consent. To let an agent work on a second brand, connect it again and pick that brand. A client can never reach a brand it was not granted.

facts.title: Codes and Refresh Tokens Are Single Use
facts.body: Authorization codes live ten minutes and are consumed atomically, so a replayed code fails. Refresh tokens are rotated on every use and stored hashed. Idle client registrations expire after 180 days.

mcp.endpointsDescription: For anyone building an MCP client or auditing the flow. All of it is discoverable from the two well-known documents; nothing here needs to be configured by hand.

connect.title: Pick your agent. Three steps, then it can post.
connect.intro: Every client below reaches the same hosted MCP server. Most sign in through the browser: the first tool call opens a consent page where you pick the workspace and the brand the agent may act on, and the client receives a key bound to that brand. Clients that cannot open a browser take a workspace API key instead. Same server, same permissions, same list in Settings.

common.adminRequired: You are a workspace owner or admin with a verified email, on a workspace with an active plan and at least one brand.
common.preferSignIn: Prefer the sign-in. Use a key only where the client cannot open a browser.
common.verifyTool: Ask the agent to call list_products. It should answer with the one brand you granted and its connected channels.
common.verifySettings: The connection is listed in Settings, API with a Connected Agent badge, its last-used time, and its request volume. Revoke it there at any time.
common.oneClickHint: Opens the app and adds the server. Paste the JSON below if the link does not open.

claude-code.label: Claude Code
claude-code.summary: The plugin installs the skill and the hosted server together. Nothing to configure, nothing to paste.
before: Claude Code is installed and signed in to your Anthropic account.
add: Run the two plugin commands in any terminal, or add just the server with the third command.
signIn: Ask Claude anything about Markaestro, or run /mcp and choose markaestro.
Your browser opens the consent page. Pick the workspace and brand, review the permissions, click Allow.
To switch brands later, run /mcp again, sign out, and sign in with the other brand.

claude.label: Claude
claude.summary: claude.ai and Claude Desktop take the server URL as a custom connector and sign in through the same consent page.
before: Custom connectors are available on paid Claude plans. On Team and Enterprise an owner may need to enable them.
add: Open Settings, Connectors, then Add custom connector.
Paste the server URL below, leave the OAuth client fields empty, and click Add.
signIn: Click Connect next to Markaestro. The consent page opens in a new tab.
Pick the workspace and brand, review the permissions, click Allow. The tab closes and the connector shows as connected.
In a chat, enable Markaestro from the tools menu when you want the agent to use it.

cursor.label: Cursor
cursor.summary: One click adds the server to Cursor. The first tool call opens the browser sign-in; Cursor keeps the token in your OS keychain.
before: Cursor with MCP enabled. Remote MCP servers work on every Cursor plan.
add: Click Add to Cursor and confirm the install prompt in Cursor.
Or paste the JSON into .cursor/mcp.json in a project (shared with your team through git) or ~/.cursor/mcp.json (just you).
signIn: Open Cursor Settings, Tools & MCP. Markaestro shows Needs login; click it.
Your browser opens the consent page. Pick the workspace and brand, click Allow. Cursor picks up the token and lists the tools.
Grok Bot inside Cursor uses this same server entry.

captions.headless: For a shared build machine or CI, a workspace API key in the headers replaces the sign-in.

chatgpt.label: ChatGPT
chatgpt.summary: ChatGPT connects to Markaestro as a custom app in Developer mode and signs in through the consent page.
before: Developer mode needs ChatGPT Pro, Business, Enterprise, or Edu. Pro exposes read-only tools; Business, Enterprise, and Edu expose all of them.
On Business, Enterprise, and Edu an admin may need to allow custom apps for the workspace.
add: Open Settings, Apps & Connectors, Advanced settings, and turn on Developer mode.
Back in Apps & Connectors, click Create. Name it Markaestro, paste the server URL, choose OAuth for authentication, then click Scan Tools.
signIn: The consent page opens while ChatGPT scans the tools. Pick the workspace and brand, click Allow, then click Create.
In a chat, click the plus button, More, then Markaestro to make the tools available.
ChatGPT registers itself with Markaestro once per connection. Reconnecting creates a new connection you can revoke separately.

grok.label: Grok
grok.summary: Grok reaches Markaestro three ways: as a custom connector on grok.com, from the Grok Build terminal, and as a remote MCP tool in the xAI API.
before: grok.com connectors work on personal plans. Grok Business and Enterprise need a team admin to provision the connector.
The xAI API path runs server-side, so it always uses a workspace API key.
add: grok.com: open grok.com/connectors, click New Connector, choose Custom, and paste the server URL. If the dialog asks for a client id, use the values below.
Grok Build: run the two commands in a terminal. Grok Build also picks up a Markaestro entry from Claude Code's .mcp.json or Cursor's mcp.json.
xAI API: add the tool block to the tools array of a Responses API request.
signIn: grok.com and Grok Build open the consent page on the first tool call. Pick the workspace and brand, click Allow.
For the xAI API, create a workspace API key and pass it in the authorization field.

grok-bot.label: Grok Bot
grok-bot.summary: Grok Bot runs on a cloud computer and takes custom MCP servers with a static key. The beta has no browser sign-in for custom servers yet.
before: Grok Bot is in early beta on SuperGrok plans and inside Cursor Pro. Enterprise access is by waitlist.
You have a workspace API key with the agent scopes. Create one with the button below.
add: Open your Bot's connector settings and add a custom MCP server.
Paste the server URL, then add the key as a header using the values below.
signIn: Create a key scoped to one brand with an expiry. Store it only in the Bot's connector settings, never in a chat message.
If Grok Bot adds browser sign-in for custom servers, remove the header and reconnect. The sign-in path already works on this server.

captions.key: Header values for the connector dialog

openclaw.label: OpenClaw
openclaw.summary: OpenClaw adds remote MCP servers from its CLI and completes the sign-in on a loopback port, so it works on the machine that runs your gateway.
before: OpenClaw is installed and the gateway is running.
A headless server can finish the sign-in with the --code fallback.
add: Run the three commands, or add the server block to ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json.
Once the Markaestro skill is on ClawHub, openclaw skills install markaestro adds the agent instructions too.
signIn: openclaw mcp login markaestro prints the sign-in URL and waits on a loopback port.
Open the URL, pick the workspace and brand, click Allow. OpenClaw stores the credentials outside the config file.
Run openclaw mcp reload so running agents pick up the tools.

hermes.label: Hermes
hermes.summary: Hermes Agent registers HTTP MCP servers from config.yaml and runs the sign-in itself, storing the token under ~/.hermes/mcp-tokens.
before: Hermes Agent is installed. Secrets belong in ~/.hermes/.env and are referenced as ${VAR} in config.
add: Add the mcp_servers block to ~/.hermes/config.yaml.
In a running session, send /reload-mcp. The tools appear as mcp_markaestro_<tool>.
signIn: On the first tool call Hermes opens the consent page. Pick the workspace and brand, click Allow.
Hermes refreshes the token on its own. Revoke it from Settings, API when you are done.

generic.label: Other MCP Client
generic.summary: Any client that speaks Streamable HTTP and OAuth 2.1 with dynamic client registration connects with the server URL alone.
before: The client supports remote MCP servers over Streamable HTTP and can open a browser for OAuth. If it cannot, use the API Key tab.
add: Add the server URL in the client's MCP configuration. The JSON below is the common mcpServers shape.
Do not configure a client id or secret. The client registers itself on first use.
signIn: The first tool call is answered with a sign-in challenge and the client opens the consent page.
Pick the workspace and brand, click Allow. The client exchanges the code for a brand-bound key and refreshes it every 30 days.

headless.label: API Key
headless.summary: For CI jobs, cron workers, and clients that cannot open a browser: a workspace API key in the Authorization header reaches the same server with the same permissions.
before: You can create keys: workspace owner or admin with a verified email.
add: Create a key bound to one brand with only the scopes the agent needs and an expiry.
Pass it as a bearer header on the hosted server, or as MARKAESTRO_API_KEY to the local stdio server, which can also upload files from disk.
signIn: Store the key in the agent's secret store, never in a prompt or a repository.
Rotate or revoke it in Settings, API. Every key shows its last-used time and request volume.
